title: Ashtpadi 17, salok: true in the beginning
hook: aad sach: the same salok as Japji's opening returns (Sukhmani 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 16, and your line: formless, everywhere. Did you notice the space of a room before its things? Today the seventeenth ashtpadi opens with words you've heard before. Day five hundred two.

You're halfway through a long, new song, and suddenly the band plays the opening bars of a song you've known since childhood. It stops you. You know where you are. Something like that happens at the seventeenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani. After sixteen ashtpadis of Guru Arjan's own words, the salok here is a line that Sikhs know from the very first page of the Guru Granth Sahib, the line right after the Mool Mantar, which opens Japji Sahib every morning. Words Sikhs know as Guru Nanak's, coming back inside Guru Arjan's hymn. Today: true in the beginning.
screen: `A NEW SONG, THEN AN OLD ONE.` → `THE FIRST PAGE OF THE GURU.` → `GURU NANAK'S WORDS RETURN.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in Punjabi first, because many Sikhs know it by heart. Aad sach, jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach, Nanak, hosee bhee sach. In paraphrase: true in the beginning, true through the ages. True now, Nanak, and true it will be. Sach is truth, and in Gurbani it means more than not lying. Sach is what's real, what lasts, what holds. And the line walks it through every kind of time. Aad: the beginning, before anything began. Jugaad: through the ages, the long eras of the world. Hai bhee: is, right now. Hosee bhee: will be, after everything we know is gone. Four steps, and the truth is the same at every one. Why would Guru Arjan bring it back here? Sukhmani doesn't say, and the sources don't record his reason, so we can only notice what it does. It ties the hymn to the root of the scripture. Sukhmani was composed by the fifth Guru; Japji by the first. Placing the same salok in both says these are one voice, one teaching, passed from Guru to Guru like one flame lit from another. Sikhs often describe the Gurus exactly that way: ten bodies, one light. It also does something for anyone reciting Sukhmani, which takes over an hour. Deep in the middle, when attention is fading, here is a line the tongue already knows. You come home to it. And it sets up what follows. The seventeenth ashtpadi is about truth, and it starts by saying truth is not something that changes with the times. True then. True now.
screen: `AAD SACH, JUGAAD SACH.` · `BEGINNING, AGES, NOW, TO COME.` · `ONE LIGHT, GURU TO GURU.` · `A LINE THE TONGUE KNOWS.` · then, large: `TRUE THEN, TRUE NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say aad sach once, slowly, and then sit with it. Aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, hosee bhee sach. If the Punjabi is new to you, just say: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, true to come. Then let it settle. Think of one thing in your life that was true at the start and is still true now. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 17. Its salok is Japji's: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, hosee bhee sach. True in the beginning, through the ages, now, and to come.
Your line: true then, true now. Today, when the news or your mood shifts fast, say aad sach to yourself, and remember what doesn't shift. Day five hundred two.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite aad sach, jugaad sach as the salok after the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji Sahib each morning, and meet the same salok again at the opening of Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi.

what a scholar hears: the salok appears both after the Mool Mantar (Ang 1) and at Sukhmani 17 (Ang 285), and the four-fold aad, jugaad, hai, hosee covers all of time.

Attribution: the Japji salok is traditionally Guru Nanak's, while Sukhmani as a whole is Guru Arjan's (Mahala 5); hook softened to 'words Sikhs know as Guru Nanak's'. Keeper to confirm how to present the shared salok's authorship.
